paragraphs: I've been working in Lafayette long enough to know Reliez Valley well, and a property like 15 Surmont Ct stands out immediately  -  a 0.73-acre court lot with Mount Diablo views, an in-law suite, a pool, a sports court, and open-beam ceilings that most buyers have to travel out of state to find. When I saw the listing come off the market after 62 days without a sale, I wanted to reach out, because that outcome doesn't match what this home actually is.

What the listing history tells me is that the strategy ran out of runway before the right buyers were found. At $514 per square foot, this home was priced well below the Lafayette range for a property with this footprint, setting, and amenity stack  -  which means the conversation wasn't about the price at all. It was about reach and narrative. The Mount Diablo view from that wrap-around deck, the in-law suite with its own separate living areas, the sports court, the three fireplaces  -  those are specific details that a certain kind of buyer is actively looking for. A standard listing approach often treats features like those as a bullet-point list rather than the center of the story.

I've put together a short analysis of where I think the friction was, along with how I'd approach a relaunch differently  -  what the pricing position actually signals, which buyer profiles this home is built for, and what a full-coverage campaign would look like to reach them. It's in the pages behind this letter.
If you're already working with an agent toward a new listing, please feel free to set this aside  -  no hard feelings. If you're not, I'd welcome a short conversation whenever you're ready.

cover.tagline: The Blueprint for a Successful Sale

exec_summary.headline: A Rare Reliez Valley Estate with Views, Versatility, and Three Levels of Living  -  and a Listing That Left Most of That on the Table
exec_summary.p1: 15 Surmont Ct is a genuinely uncommon property in the Lafayette inventory. Positioned at the end of a private court on nearly three-quarters of an acre, it offers sweeping Mount Diablo views, a pool with sundeck, a lighted sports court, three fireplaces, and a fully self-contained in-law or au pair suite on the lower level  -  all within ten minutes of downtown Lafayette and BART. The open-beam ceilings in the main living room, the Shoji screens, the six-burner Dacor range, and the wrap-around deck create a home that reads as a lifestyle property, not just a square-footage play. Buyers in this price range who are looking for that combination  -  private lot, views, multi-generational flexibility, and outdoor amenities  -  have very few options in Lafayette. This home checks every one of those boxes.
exec_summary.p2: The listing ran 62 days and came off the market without a sale. That gap between the home's actual asset base and the outcome it produced points to a strategy problem, not a property problem. At $514 per square foot, the home was priced at the low end of the Lafayette range for a fixer-tier property  -  and this is not a fixer. The marketing didn't resolve that disconnect. A buyer comparing this home against other Lafayette listings at this price point needed to understand, specifically and visually, what justified the number and what the number actually represented relative to the market. That case was never fully made.
exec_summary.p3: A relaunch needs to do one thing well: make the Mount Diablo views, the multi-level flexibility, and the private court setting feel real to buyers who are researching online from San Francisco and the East Bay before they ever schedule a showing. That starts with the visual package and the narrative, and it ends with active distribution to the buyers who are already looking for exactly this.

forensics.title: Friction #1: Stale Listing Psychology After 62 Days
forensics.body: Once a listing crosses the 45-day mark, buyer behavior shifts in a specific and measurable way. Buyers stop evaluating the home on its merits and start asking why it hasn't sold. After 62 days on market, that question had become louder than the Mount Diablo views, the pool, or the in-law suite. The stigma wasn't earned  -  it was created by a strategy that didn't actively find the right buyers before the clock ran out. The buyers for a property like this don't browse passively on Zillow; they need to be reached where they're actually looking, and reached before they've already made a decision about another home.
forensics.brightwork_contrast: BrightWork runs geo-targeted digital campaigns into San Francisco and the East Bay, reaching buyers who are actively researching Lafayette relocations before they've identified a specific property  -  so the right audience finds this home before the market clock becomes the story.

forensics.title: Friction #2: The View and the Setting Were Never Shown
forensics.body: A home with sweeping Mount Diablo views from a wrap-around deck, a private 0.73-acre court lot, and a pool and sports court below is a property that lives or dies on its photography and aerial context. Standard MLS angles  -  front elevation and interior room shots  -  leave the lot position, the hillside setting, and the panoramic view invisible to online buyers. A buyer researching from San Francisco or Oakland cannot tell from a flat exterior photo that this home sits at the end of a private court with an open-sky view to the east. That visual gap is why qualified buyers scroll past without booking a showing.
forensics.brightwork_contrast: BrightWork's Sky Tour gives buyers the aerial context that ground photography cannot  -  lot position, court setting, hillside backdrop, and the relationship between the home and the view it commands  -  before they ever step inside.

forensics.title: Friction #3: A Complex, Multi-Level Home With No Digital Walk-Through
forensics.body: A three-level home with two family rooms, a self-contained lower-level in-law suite, a primary suite with private deck, and distinct indoor-outdoor flow on the main level is genuinely difficult to convey through a photo gallery. Buyers comparing multiple properties at this price point need to understand the layout and the flow before they commit to a 30-minute drive to Reliez Valley. Without a way to walk the home digitally, busy professionals and out-of-area buyers default to simpler, easier-to-understand listings  -  not because this home is harder to love, but because it's harder to picture. That friction cost this listing real showings.
forensics.brightwork_contrast: A 3D Matterport tour lets buyers walk every level of this home from anywhere  -  including the lower-level suite and the primary deck  -  so the layout is understood and the home is already familiar before they schedule a showing.

positioning_table.verdict: At $514/sqft versus a benchmark range of $650-$720/sqft, this home sits near the lower end of that range. At $514 per square foot, 15 Surmont Ct was listed well below the low end of the Lafayette fixer range  -  and this home is not a fixer. The lot, the views, the in-law suite, the pool, and the outdoor amenity package place it solidly in renovated or premium territory, where comparable Lafayette properties trade between $780 and $920 per square foot. That pricing position was a real advantage, but only if buyers understood what they were getting at that number. The strategy needed to build that case clearly and deliver it to the right audience  -  and that's exactly where the opportunity remains.

pillars.title: Pillar I  -  Reach the Buyers Who Are Already Looking for This
pillars.body: The buyers for a Mount Diablo view home with a private court lot, pool, and in-law suite are not browsing randomly  -  they know what they want, and they're researching Lafayette from San Francisco and the East Bay before they make a move. BrightWork's geo-targeted digital campaigns put this home directly in front of that audience, in the channels where they're actually spending time, before they've committed to something else. Passive MLS distribution wasn't enough for this property. Active distribution is.

pillars.title: Pillar II  -  Build the Visual Package This Home Deserves
pillars.body: A 0.73-acre hillside court lot with panoramic views and a multi-level layout is one of the harder properties to represent in a standard photo set  -  and one of the most important to get right. The relaunch starts with a Sky Tour to establish the setting and the views from the air, a 3D Matterport walk-through so buyers can move through all three levels digitally, and cinematic interior photography that gives the open-beam ceilings and the wrap-around deck the presence they carry in person. More informed buyers means fewer wasted showings and stronger offers.

pillars.title: Pillar III  -  Price Position Needs a Narrative, Not Just a Number
pillars.body: At $514 per square foot against a Lafayette market that runs from $650 to over $900 for comparable-quality homes, this listing had a compelling value story to tell  -  and it never told it. A buyer who sees the number without the context either questions what's wrong or moves on. BrightWork's listing strategy pairs the pricing data with a direct, specific explanation of what the buyer is getting relative to the market  -  so the number feels like an opportunity, not a question mark. That's the conversation that turns interest into showings.
